title: Contemplating the Mind
author: Compiled and expounded by Zhanran
excerpt: (Excerpted from White Cloud Essentials of Mind (The Precious Book of Mind Contemplation))

inline.s: (Excerpted from
White Cloud Essentials of Mind (The Precious Book of Mind Contemplation)
Within the three realms, the mind is lord.
Those who can contemplate the mind are finally freed;
those who cannot remain forever bound.
In idle talk, speak no one's faults; in quiet sitting, watch only your own mind.
The ancients said
If one does not contemplate the mind, the Dharma has no place from which to come."

For the Buddha-Dharma rests wholly upon the pure mind; only by turning the light around and reflecting within can the Buddha-nature be drawn forth, and then all gates of samadhi, all gates of dharani, all gates of liberation, and all gates of spiritual power appear at once. Thus we know that the mind is the source from which the wondrous Dharma comes; if one does not contemplate the mind, how can it be drawn out? Therefore mind contemplation is the foremost wondrous practice of the Buddha-Dharma, and no other practice can match it.
[The gate of dharani] Dharani is Sanskrit;
translated into Chinese it is
total retention.
Because

by the dharma of total retention the bodhisattva accords with the speech and voices of all living beings, guides them to right faith, causes them to put an end to all evil thoughts and to practice all wholesome dharmas — this is the bodhisattva's gate of dharani.
In the Mahayana Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground, the Buddha says:
"This dharma
(mind contemplation)

is called the supreme secret mind-ground dharma gate of all the Tathagatas of the ten directions; this dharma is called the gate of sudden enlightenment by which all ordinary beings enter the Tathagata's ground; this dharma is called, for all bodhisattvas who go toward great bodhi,
the true and right road

; this dharma is called the subtle jewel palace in which the Buddhas of the three times enjoy the bliss of the Dharma for themselves, and this dharma is called the inexhaustible treasure-house that benefits all sentient beings.
Good sons,
within the three realms, the mind is lord. Those who can contemplate the mind are finally freed; those who cannot remain forever bound."
The Nirvāṇa Sutra says:
"To be able to contemplate the mind-nature is called the supreme concentration."
Daoxin, the Fourth Patriarch of the Chan school, says:

"The hundred thousand dharma gates all return to the square inch; virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges all rest in the source of the mind. All gates of precepts, of concentration, and of wisdom, together with spiritual powers and transformations, are complete in themselves and never apart from your mind."
Hongren, the Fifth Patriarch, says:
"If you do not know your own mind, studying the Dharma brings no benefit."
Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch, says:

"Good friends, if one does not awaken, the Buddha is a living being; when a single thought awakens, the living being is a Buddha. Therefore know that all dharmas are within one's own mind. Why not, from within the mind, suddenly see the true suchness of your own nature? The Sutra of Bodhisattva Precepts says: 'My original self-nature is pure; if one knows one's own mind and sees the nature, all accomplish the Buddha-way.' The Vimalakirti Sutra says: 'At once suddenly opened, one returns to one's own mind.' Good friends, before Master Ren I heard the teaching but once and was awakened on the spot, suddenly seeing the true suchness of my own nature. Therefore I cause this teaching to spread, so that students of the Way may suddenly awaken to bodhi. Let each contemplate his own mind and see his own nature."
Therefore the root of the Buddha-Dharma is the mind, and the root of practice is contemplation.
To observe constantly is for prajna to perfume ignorance.
The moment ignorance is broken, the dharmakaya suddenly appears. In one leap one enters directly the ground of the Tathagata; without passing through asankhya kalpas one attains the dharmakaya.
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
"All Tathagatas, from the very ground of their initial resolve, rely upon the perfect illumination of the pure enlightened mark, forever cut off ignorance, and only then accomplish the Buddha-way."

Moreover, to arouse the bodhi mind is to contemplate the pure mind of self-nature (see in detail the previous chapter, "Arousing the Bodhi Mind"). The merit of arousing the bodhi mind is incomparably supreme and cannot be fully described. For example:
"One who arouses the bodhi mind is granted the prediction of Buddhahood by all Buddhas and is blessed by all Buddhas."

That at the first arousal of the mind the Buddhas grant the prediction is stated plainly in many sutras, such as the Sutra of the Arising of Bodhi, the Mahayana Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground, and the Sutra of Excellent Thought; the fullest account is in the Avatamsaka Sutra. As for the blessing of the Buddhas, the Lankavatara Sutra says:
"In every land throughout the ten directions, the Buddhas beyond all measure stretch forth their hands of light and stroke the crown of that one's head."
Thus do all Buddhas constantly bless such a practitioner. (See in detail the section "The Merit of Arousing the Mind" in the previous chapter.)

Our Buddha taught the Dharma for forty-nine years, in more than three hundred and sixty assemblies; the teachings differ in a thousand ways, yet their final home is not two. In a single phrase: it is the one mind alone (the one mind is the true mind). Not to understand the one mind is to posit an external world, and from this arise delusion and karma, and the wheel of rebirth turns without end. If one truly understands the one mind, then the three insights, the six spiritual powers, the ten powers, and the four fearlessnesses come of themselves without being sought. Hence it is said: among all dharmas, the mind is foremost. Whoever studies the Dharma and drifts along with objects, not taking mind contemplation as the foundation, is an outsider.

[The three insights] The insight of past lives, the insight of the heavenly eye, and the insight of the extinction of outflows. The insight of past lives is the clear knowledge of all the past lives of oneself or others; the insight of the heavenly eye is the clear knowledge of all the future lives of oneself or others; the insight of the extinction of outflows is the severing of all afflictions by means of sagely wisdom. [The six spiritual powers] The spiritual powers attained by the sages of the Three Vehicles are six in number: the power of the heavenly eye, the power of the heavenly ear, the power of knowing the minds of others, the power of knowing past lives, the power of unimpeded movement, and the power of the extinction of outflows. [The ten powers] These are the ten powers possessed by the Tathagata. 1. The power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible, that is, the power to know the reasonableness and the unreasonableness of all things; 2. the power of knowing the karmic retributions of the three times, that is, the power to know the causal retributions throughout the three times of all living beings; 3. the power of knowing all meditations, liberations, and samadhis, that is, the power to know all dhyanas, liberations, samadhis, and the like; 4. the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties of living beings, that is, the power to know the sharpness or dullness of living beings' faculties and the greatness or smallness of the fruits they attain; 5. the power of knowing various understandings, that is, the power to know universally the different understandings of living beings; 6. the power of knowing various realms, that is, the power to know universally the different realms of living beings; 7. the power of knowing where all paths lead, that is, the power to know the causes and effects of the paths walked by all living beings; 8. the power of the unobstructed heavenly eye, that is, the power to see with the heavenly eye, without obstruction, the birth and death of living beings and the karmic causes of their good and evil; 9. the power of knowing past lives and the taintless, that is, the power to know the past lives of living beings and to know taintless nirvāṇa; 10. the power of knowing the eternal cutting off of habitual tendencies, that is, the power to know truly and as it is that the residual traces of all deluded afflictions are forever cut off and never arise again. [The four fearlessnesses] 1. Fearlessness in all wisdom: in the midst of the assembly the Buddha declares plainly that he is a person of all wisdom, without any fear. 2. Fearlessness in the extinction of outflows: in the midst of the assembly the Buddha declares plainly that he has cut off all afflictions, without any fear. 3. Fearlessness in teaching the dharmas that obstruct the Way: in the midst of the assembly the Buddha teaches the dharmas of delusion, karma, and other obstructions, without any fear. 4. Fearlessness in teaching the Way that ends suffering: in the midst of the assembly the Buddha teaches the right Way of precepts, concentration, and wisdom that ends all suffering, without any fear.
Bodhidharma, the founding patriarch, says in his Treatise on Breaking the Marks:
"Question: If there be a person who aspires to the Buddha-way, what dharma should he practice to be most concise and essential? Answer:
The single dharma of mind contemplation alone encompasses all dharmas and is the most concise and essential.

Question: How can one dharma encompass all dharmas? Answer: The mind is the root of all dharmas; all dharmas are produced by the mind alone. If one understands the mind, then all dharmas are complete, just as with a great tree: all its branches, flowers, and fruits depend entirely upon the root. He who plants a tree keeps the root, and only then does it bear fruit; he who fells a tree removes the root, and it must surely die. If one understands the mind and cultivates the Way, little effort brings easy success; if one does not understand the mind and cultivates, effort is wasted and there is no benefit. Therefore know that all good and evil come from one's own mind. To seek elsewhere, apart from the mind, is in the end to have no ground at all."

First one must still the mind and rest the thoughts: set aside completely the six dusts and the ten thousand conditions; give no thought to good or evil matters; do not think at all of past or future. Look directly at the present thought as it flits to and fro, arising and ceasing without pause; do not grasp it, do not follow it, do not cut it off. Simply watch it quietly and closely. When a deluded thought arises, the moment you look it is gone without a trace; when it arises again, watch it in the same way; if no thought arises, just watch the watching.

When after long practice it becomes second nature, and you watch until not a single thought arises, you are then in accord with prajna. (This is contemplation without thought, thoughtless contemplation.) The
Treatise on Arousing the Bodhi Mind says:
"When the deluded mind arises
(when a deluded thought arises)
, know it and do not follow it; when the deluded
thought subsides
(when the deluded thought subsides)
, the source of the mind is empty and still, all virtues are complete, and its wondrous functions are inexhaustible."

Such is the wonder of the mind-nature. That in ordinary life we are out of accord with it is because we are obscured by deluded thoughts, and this is the ignorant mind. On what does ignorance depend? It arises in dependence upon suchness. To contemplate the ignorant mind is to contemplate the mind of suchness; to contemplate the mind-nature is to contemplate the ignorant mind. Why? Because suchness is the substance of thought, and thought is the function of suchness. To contemplate and thereby attain concentration is the samadhi of suchness, the king of samadhis, and therefore it is called the supreme concentration.

[Know it and do not follow it] Watch the thought without judging it, and do not let it continue (do not let thought give rise to further thought). The key to "knowing it and not following it" is to work at the "knowing": watch as a cat watches a mouse hole, so that the moment a thought arises you know it. Once you can "know it the moment it arises," the "not following" becomes easy. [The source of the mind] The mind is the source of all dharmas, and so it is called the source of the mind. [All virtues are complete] The word si means "thereby, then"; all virtues are thereby complete. For example: "With preparation, one may then be free from harm."
The essential formula of mind contemplation:

Whenever a thought arises, know it and do not follow it. Neither like nor dislike, neither grasp nor reject, do not set about correcting it; only still the mind and observe closely. This is prajna perfuming ignorance, and the transformation from ordinary being to sage takes place of itself.
Not to know is to lack wisdom; to follow is to lack concentration. To know and not follow is to hold concentration and wisdom in equal measure.
The first task of mind contemplation:
know it and do not follow it, and purify the flowing stream of deluded thoughts in your own mind.
Question: The method of contemplation for cultivating the practice of no-thought in the Mahayana method of calm abiding and insight is this:

"When a thought arises, observe it at once; at the very moment of observing, the preceding thought has already ceased and the following thought has not yet arisen, and in the present there is no thought."
This method is precisely the contemplation of no-thought. What does the master think of it?
Answer: This differs somewhat from my own view. My basis is the verse from the sutra, which says:
"Behold this mind of yours: thought after thought, forever arising and ceasing, like an illusion, having nothing whatsoever, and yet the great reward is won."

This is the true arousing of the bodhi mind; this is the practice of no-thought, no-abiding, and no-marks. (Editor's note: The former method focuses on the blank interval of no-thought and calls that the practice of no-thought. The latter method focuses on contemplating that thoughts have no self-nature, knowing them and not following them — being thoughtless amid thought — and calls that the practice of no-thought. The difference between the two methods is subtle, and yet it is the crucial point. The latter method is superior to the former.)
Question: In contemplating the mind, should one investigate where deluded thoughts arise?

Answer: To investigate where deluded thoughts arise — those words are quite wrong! For investigation requires the use of the intellect. This method of mind contemplation is apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness; how could there be any reason to use consciousness? Just look directly, and that is enough; there is no need to investigate. The ancients said: When the light of the mind shines through, the remaining flaws vanish of themselves. How concise and essential! Why bother with inquiry?
Question: Why do you say, "Just look directly, and that is enough"?

Editor's answer: This is a method of contemplation apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness. So long as the contemplation is focused, no deluded thought arises ("when the light of the mind shines through, the remaining flaws vanish of themselves"), and because the power of awareness grows rapidly, it will of itself blossom and bear fruit.

Question: On what sutra is this method of mind contemplation based? You often cite the Mind-Ground Contemplation Sutra. Is it perhaps based on that sutra? Yet what that sutra teaches is the contemplation of the moon wheel. Why, instead of having us contemplate the moon, do you have us contemplate the mind? This doubt has not yet been cleared up; I beg you to instruct me.
Answer:

1. As to the sutra relied upon. Every method of contemplation must accord with the meaning of the sutras. The method I have given you relies on the Lankavatara Sutra, not on the Mind-Ground Contemplation Sutra. The Mind-Ground Contemplation Sutra explains the method of mind contemplation in the greatest detail, and I cite it as evidence. In truth, this Tathagata Chan takes the Lankavatara as its foundation, and it was with this that Bodhidharma transmitted the mind. The Tang translation of the Lankavatara Sutra (that is, the Mahayana Sutra of Entry into Lanka), in its third fascicle, says:

"Mahasattva Bodhisattva Mahamati again spoke to the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, may it please you to teach the marks of the practice that realizes sagely wisdom, and the marks of the practice of the One Vehicle, so that I and the bodhisattva mahasattvas may attain this skill and, within the Buddha-Dharma, awaken without relying on others.' The Buddha said: 'Listen well; I shall tell you.' Mahamati said: 'So be it.' The Buddha said: 'Mahamati, the bodhisattva mahasattva, relying on the teachings of the sages, is without discrimination. Dwelling alone in quiet seclusion, he observes self-realization; not awakening through others, free from the view of discrimination, he rises higher and higher and enters the ground of the Tathagata. Such cultivation is called the marks of the practice of self-realized sagely wisdom. What is called the marks of the practice of the One Vehicle? It means the attainment of the realization of the way of the One Vehicle. What is called knowing the way of the One Vehicle? It means being free from the discriminations of the grasping and the grasped, and abiding as it really is. Mahamati, this way of the One Vehicle, except for the Tathagata, cannot be attained by outsiders, by the Two Vehicles, by Brahma kings, or by the like.'"

This sutra is the mainstay; you must not doubt it. If one cites the Lankavatara, the evidence is very abundant. But its text is profound and expansive, and not easy to understand. Therefore I take the chapter on mind contemplation as evidence, since this is the common meaning of the Vaipulya teachings.

[Vaipulya] Fang means "vast" and deng means "equal": in the third period the Buddha taught extensively the four teachings — the Tripitaka, the Shared, the Distinct, and the Perfect — benefiting equally those of sharp and those of dull faculties, and therefore it is called vaipulya. [The four teachings] These are the four teachings of the transforming doctrine: the Tripitaka teaching, the Shared teaching, the Distinct teaching, and the Perfect teaching. The above four — Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect — are the gates by which living beings are taught and transformed, and therefore they are called the transforming doctrine. The Tripitaka teaching is the three baskets of sutras, vinaya, and abhidharma, clearly divided into categories; it teaches the four truths of arising and ceasing by causes and conditions, its primary aim being to teach the hearers and the solitary realizers, while it transforms bodhisattvas incidentally. The Shared teaching teaches the four true truths of emptiness and non-arising, so that the Three Vehicles study it in common, though bodhisattvas are its primary recipients and the Two Vehicles its secondary. The Distinct teaching teaches the limitless dharmas of the Great Vehicle specifically to bodhisattvas, and does not extend to the Two Vehicles. The Perfect teaching teaches the Middle Way and true reality, in which phenomena and principle are perfectly interfused, to bodhisattvas of the sharpest faculties. [The four truths] The truth of suffering, the truth of origination, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path. 1. The truth of suffering is the truth that explains that life is full of suffering. Suffering has the mark of oppression. Life has three sufferings, eight sufferings, and immeasurable sufferings; suffering is the reality of actual human life. 2. The origination of the truth of origination means to bring about or to cause; it is the truth that explains how the suffering of life comes about. The suffering of life arises because, out of craving, one creates karma, and so one suffers and transmigrates. 3. The truth of cessation is the truth that explains the stilling of all suffering. When all the origination of suffering, that is, craving, is forever cut off without remainder, with no defilement and no attachment, one no longer suffers or transmigrates; this is the truth of cessation. 4. The truth of the path is the truth that explains how to forever cut off the origination of suffering, that is, craving — in other words, the path that ends suffering, the Noble Eightfold Path. Among the Four Noble Truths, origination is the cause and suffering is the fruit; the path is the cause and cessation is the fruit.

[The five periods of the Buddha's teaching] After his enlightenment, in the first twenty-one days the Buddha taught the Avatamsaka Sutra and brought the great bodhisattvas across; this is the Avatamsaka period. Then at Deer Park and elsewhere, over twelve years, he taught the Agama sutras of the Lesser Vehicle and brought across those of the hearer and solitary-realizer vehicles; this is the Agama period. After the Agama period, over eight years, he taught the Vimalakirti, Srimala, Golden Light, and other great Mahayana sutras, speaking broadly of the four teachings and benefiting all capacities equally; this is the Vaipulya period. Thereafter, over twenty-two years, he taught the various divisions of the Prajna sutras, emphasizing the meaning that all dharmas are empty; this is the Prajna period. In the last eight years he taught the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma, gathering the Three Vehicles into the One Buddha Vehicle. After the Lotus, as the Buddha was about to enter nirvāṇa, in the city of Kushinagara, between the twin sala trees, in a single day and night he taught the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra, revealing the meaning of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and showing that all living beings have the Buddha-nature, and that even icchantikas shall become Buddhas; this is the Lotus-Nirvāṇa period. There is a verse that describes the course of the five periods: the Avatamsaka first, twenty-one days; the Agamas twelve, the Vaipulya eight; twenty-two years of Prajna teaching; the Lotus and Nirvāṇa together eight years.

2. Why the contemplation of the moon wheel is not taught. This dharma gate is straightforward and sets aside expedient means, whereas the moon-wheel contemplation employs expedient means: this is the first difference. This dharma gate is a method of no-marks, whereas the moon-wheel contemplation has marks: the second difference. This dharma gate is apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness, whereas the moon-wheel contemplation makes exclusive use of the six consciousnesses: the third difference. This dharma gate is free from the grasping and the grasped, whereas in the moon-wheel contemplation the grasper and the grasped are plainly present, the very opposite: the fourth difference. This dharma gate enters directly the ocean of the nature of suchness, whereas the beginner in the moon-wheel contemplation enters a realm of solitary shadows: the fifth difference. With these five differences, the gulf between them is as between heaven and earth. They must not be cultivated together. The establishment of the moon-wheel contemplation in the Mind-Ground Contemplation Sutra is for another type of capacity, and cannot be discussed on the same footing.

[The realm of solitary shadows] Images that arise in dependence upon the thoughts and imaginings of the sixth consciousness, that is, the intellect; they have no substance whatever and are merely illusions. For example, the realm in which flowers appear in empty space or horns upon a rabbit.
Question: How does one clarify the mind and see the nature?
Answer: Bodhidharma's three phrases (
"Outwardly cut off all conditions, inwardly the mind has no panting, the mind like a wall"

), sum up everything. The Sixth Patriarch's "not thinking of good, not thinking of evil" is precisely "outwardly cutting off all conditions." "At the very moment of just this" is precisely "inwardly the mind has no panting." The words differ; how could the meaning be two? To attain "at the very moment of just this" is simply to be unmoved in one flavor; do it for one thought lasting ten thousand years, and what further dharma is there? "Which is the original face of the Venerable Ming?" is a question, and it is called springing the trigger. (In the doctrinal schools it is called the constant trigger. The Buddha-Dharma takes the mind as the trigger, and so it is said: "Turn the trigger back for a single thought, and you are the same as one who has long attained it.") The Chan school says: the ordinary person's mysterious gate is tightly shut, and the lock of consciousness is hard to open. The trigger is the mysterious gate; a master casts a single word at it, strikes the trigger, and the other is at once enlightened. But the most important part of this koan is the three words "at the moment of just this" (that is, when good and evil are not thought of), which is the secret of the Chan school. If one who has aroused the mind can abide in the mind thus, enlightenment is not far off. The patriarch says:
"'At the moment of just this,' it is called the time before the Buddha was born." It is also called: "Dwelling at the summit, precious beyond compare."

If one can abide in the mind thus for several hours in a day, that is as it should be. The causes and conditions for springing the trigger will come of themselves; there is no need for a teacher's guidance. The patriarch says:
"If only you can be at the moment of just this, you need not worry that you will not be thoroughly enlightened."
This belongs to the secret essentials of the mind-dharma, and may be put into practice with effort.
[Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil] The Sixth Patriarch says:

"If you wish to know the essentials of the mind, simply do not think of good or evil at all, and you will naturally enter the pure mind-essence, serene and eternally still, with wondrous functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
(See in detail
A Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
) [At the very moment of just this] The Sixth Patriarch says:
"Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil — at the very moment of just this, which is the original face of the Venerable Ming?"
(See in detail
A Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
Question: One who has seen the nature is free and at ease, having left the wheel of rebirth; but when he discards this illusory body, where is he reborn?

Answer: He may be reborn in any of the pure lands of the ten directions according to his vow. If he wishes to be born in the West, he will certainly attain the highest grade of the highest class. If he is not born in a pure land, he may lodge at will among humans or gods, and that is equal to a pure land.
Question: For one who has not seen the nature, how should he apply the mind at the time of death so as to escape the wheel of rebirth and gain liberation? I beg you to teach me.
Answer: One who has not seen the nature, at the time of death, should abide securely in the bodhi mind and will naturally gain liberation. (Chan Master Huangbo says:
"Simply forget the mind and be one with the dharma realm, and you will be at ease."
Note added by the compiler.)
Question: Will mind contemplation cause one to stagnate on the path of cultivation?

Editor's answer: If the method is correct, one will not stagnate on the path. Above it was said, "if no thought arises, just watch the watching"; the words "just watch" are the key, and this is stillness with illumination. To be still without illuminating is to stagnate on the path. Therefore, when a deluded thought arises, know it and do not follow it; when the deluded thought subsides, keep watching — this is illumination, this is awareness. The correct method of mind contemplation is: illumination with stillness, stillness with illumination. The wonder of mind contemplation lies in this: it is unceasing awareness, perfuming ignorance with prajna, until at last it becomes the great enlightenment. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
"All Tathagatas, from the very ground of their initial resolve, rely upon the perfect illumination of the pure enlightened mark, forever cut off ignorance, and only then accomplish the Buddha-way."
Question: When I contemplate the mind with focus, there is no thought; how then do I practice "knowing it and not following it"?

Editor's answer: With most people, the moment a deluded thought arises they fall into the delusion, and only after a while — sometimes quite a long while — do they realize that they have been lost in thought. Your power of awareness is already fairly strong, and so when you contemplate with focus there are no deluded thoughts; but as time goes on there will be lapses, and then a deluded thought will seize the opening and arise. To practice "knowing it and not following it" means that the moment a deluded thought arises you become aware of it at once and are master of yourself, no longer turning with the deluded thought. Practice in this way, and as the days pass and the work deepens, when your awareness is not only focused and continuous but also enduring, you will be able to dwell for long periods in the state of stillness with illumination and illumination with stillness, and further, to make motion and stillness one; this is the prelude to clarifying the mind and seeing the nature.

In general, the essential points of mind contemplation are these: when a thought is present, contemplate the thought (know it and do not follow it); when no thought is present, contemplate emptiness (stillness with illumination). The Sixth Patriarch says: "If you wish to know the essentials of the mind, simply do not think of good or evil at all, and you will naturally enter the pure mind-essence, serene and eternally still, with wondrous functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges." (The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch)
Question: When I contemplate the mind my head easily becomes dizzy. What should I do?
Editor's answer: This is because your awareness is insufficient; the foundation of mind contemplation is to have sufficient awareness. For this reason, first practice according to
The Chan of Awareness

, in its preliminary section (awareness of movement, awareness of sensation, awareness of breathing, awareness of the present moment, and awareness of thoughts), in order to cultivate sufficient awareness; then come back to mind contemplation. In addition, at the beginning it is best to contemplate the mind many times a day, for short periods each time, seeking practical effect.
Question: How does one actually accomplish "when the deluded mind arises, know it and do not follow it"?

Editor's answer: How to accomplish "when the deluded mind arises, know it and do not follow it" is the key to the work of mind contemplation, and so there have been many discussions of it through the ages. For example: the moment a thought arises, shout at it; when a thought arises, give a stark awakening; when a deluded thought arises, ask it where it came from; and so on. Another example: observe the mind's thoughts closely, and when a deluded thought arises, simply watch it and see how it will develop; if you really watch it in this way, the deluded thought will subside. If it arises again, watch it again in this way, and it will subside again. Continue thus until there is no thinking and no thought. The Sutra of the Buddha Treasury says:
"The anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas is entirely without thinking and without thought."

"Knowing it and not following it" is the result of strong awareness. Therefore one should contemplate the mind a great deal and keep awareness running without pause, in order to cultivate strong awareness. As for how to cultivate awareness, detailed discussions are found in
The Chan of Awareness
Aware Buddha-Recitation
, and
Investigative Buddha-Recitation
— the preliminary section of each.

Here is another method of mind contemplation: contemplating the mind in presence — contemplating the mind while in the state of presence. "Presence" means being in the state of awareness of the present moment, without thinking and without thought. When you are present, you have already stepped out of deluded thought. Therefore to contemplate the mind while in the state of presence is exceedingly effective.

When contemplating the mind in presence, if a deluded thought arises it is because awareness has been lost; then with a stark awakening draw awareness back, and the deluded thought subsides. Remember: when a deluded thought arises, that is karma binding the mind; to be aware of it and have it vanish, that is the mind turning karma around. Continue in this way, and when the practice deepens you will be able to remain for long periods in the state of no-thought; should a deluded thought occasionally arise, it will drift away in an instant; and further, you will remain for long periods in the state of no-thought while knowing clearly and distinctly that it is no-thought — this is what is meant by stillness with illumination and illumination with stillness.

Awareness of the present moment means being aware of whatever can be perceived at this very moment. For example: looking attentively at a tree without thinking and without thought; listening to a sound coming through the window without thinking and without thought; being aware of movement without thinking and without thought; sensing the presence of what is around you without thinking and without thought; even being aware of this very moment without thinking and without thought — all of these are the state of presence. To use this method of contemplating the mind in presence, one must first train in the skill of presence. Practice it often, both on and off the cushion, until you can enter the state of presence anywhere and at any time, even if it does not last very long.
Question: How does one train in the skill of presence?
Answer: When you study
Aware Buddha-Recitation

, the chapter "Awareness of the Present Moment" in its preliminary section is devoted precisely to presence. Moreover, the chapters in that section on awareness of movement, awareness of sensation, awareness of breathing, and awareness of thoughts are each a single aspect of the skill of presence. Now that you know what presence is, simply combine the above techniques, then extend, deepen, and consolidate them.
Question: In contemplating the mind while present, which is primary and which is auxiliary?

Answer: At the beginning take presence as primary and mind contemplation as auxiliary; in this way it is easier to sustain. When the practice deepens, take mind contemplation as primary, sustain it as well, and gradually increase the strength and depth of the contemplation. At times this situation may arise: taking mind contemplation as primary becomes difficult to carry on. Then take presence as primary and mind contemplation as auxiliary, holding the last line of defense so that no deluded thought arises. When conditions improve, return to mind contemplation as primary and presence as auxiliary.
Question: In contemplating the mind while present, should the eyes be open or closed?
Answer: Either is acceptable. The essential point of contemplating the mind while present is this: not to let a single thought slip past, and to see through every thought.
[Not letting it slip past] Not to be deceived by it. [Seeing through it] Not to be shrouded by it, not to let oneself be toyed with by it, not to take it as something real.
Question: Generally speaking, no thought arises in me, but when certain things come up I lose control, even become emotional, and afterward I cannot be calm for a long time. What should I do?

Answer: In cultivation, if one can discover a problem, one will find a way to solve it; once the problem is solved, one has taken a great step forward on the bodhi path. Therefore it is very important to discover problems in time. As for the problem you raise, there is a wondrous method: observe your thoughts, feelings, emotions, and reactions (liking and disliking, grasping and rejecting).
The
Vegetable Roots Discourse
says:
The ancients said:
Bamboo shadows sweep the steps, yet the dust lies still; the moon wheel threads the pool, yet the water bears no trace.
Our Confucians said:
Though the stream run never so swift, the scene stays still; though the blossoms fall never so thick, the mind stays at ease.
If one always holds this intent in responding to affairs and meeting people, how free and at ease are body and mind.

In ordinary times one should do this exercise often, in different situations, and when it becomes familiar it will be ready to hand the moment something happens. Doing it over and over, one will reach the state in which the mind is like a wall and no dharma can enter. Bodhidharma, the founding patriarch, says:
"Outwardly cut off all conditions, inwardly the mind has no panting, the mind like a wall — thus may one enter the Way."
Question: How does one dissolve old karma?
Answer: On this, Master Hanshan Deqing gave the following instruction:

"The ancients taught people: 'Dissolve old karma as it comes; never create new misfortune.' For living beings heavy with karma the Buddha opened the single gate of repentance, which is the most expedient means for escaping suffering. A verse says: 'All offenses are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dissolve them. If you would repent, sit upright and contemplate true reality.' This is the primary practice; all else is auxiliary expedient means.

"The self-nature of living beings is equal to the Buddha's, originally undefiled, and without any mark of birth or death, coming or going. But because of the first non-awakening, one is deluded as to one's own self-nature, and this is called ignorance. Because of ignorance, various deluded thoughts arise, with all manner of inversion, creating all manner of karma and wrongly grasping the suffering of birth and death within the three realms. All this is ignorance: not understanding one's own mind, one turns with deluded thoughts. It is like a man fast asleep who dreams all kinds of evil dreams — all manner of scenes, all manner of terror, sufferings hard to endure. When he wakes, he seeks for the affairs of the dream and cannot find them at all. Thus living beings fall into the dream of ignorance, turn with deluded thoughts and inversions, create all manner of karma, and bring suffering upon themselves. Seen with waking eyes, how could any of those inversions be found?

"But now, here within the dream of ignorance, how can old karma be dissolved? One must use the light of wisdom to shine through and break ignorance, and truly believe that one's own mind is originally pure, and not be driven by deluded thoughts and inversions; then karma will have no cause, for deluded thought is the cause of all karma. Why is this so? Because from beginningless time one has been deluded as to one's own original mind, and life after life has created all manner of karma with a deluded mind. The habits of karma accumulate within the field of the eighth consciousness, and are watered by the water of ignorance, so that these evil seeds put forth the sprouts of karma: this is the root of offense, and from it all evil karma arises.

"Now, if old karma is to be dissolved, one must first rouse the great light of wisdom to shine through and break ignorance, and not allow deluded thoughts to sprout and grow secretly in the dark. If at the very place where a deluded thought arises one cuts it off with a single thought, then the root of accumulated past karma is dissolved on the spot. Hence it is said: do not fear the arising of a thought; fear only that awareness comes too late. If the illuminating awareness is even slightly late, one is turned by it. If in daily life, at the very place where a thought arises, one is aware of it thought after thought and dissolves it thought after thought, this is what is meant by 'all offenses are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dissolve them.' For the darkness of ignorance can be broken only by wisdom, and this is what is meant by wisdom being able to dissolve them. If day and night without pause one diligently observes, never letting it pass, and at the very place where deluded thoughts arise investigates thoroughly until there is no mark of arising at all — look and look again, and in the end it cannot be found. When after long practice it becomes second nature, one's own mind is pure and without anything; a mind without anything is true reality. If one constantly contemplates this mind, what deluded thought could remain, what karma could lodge there?"

blocks.text: 3. What Mind Is to Be Contemplated

inline.s: A Treatise on Arousing the Bodhi Mind says:
"When the deluded mind arises, know it and do not follow it; when it subsides, the source of the mind is empty and still, all virtues are complete, and its wondrous functions are inexhaustible."

Such is the wonder of the mind-nature. That we are ordinarily out of accord with it is because we are obscured by deluded thought, which is the ignorant mind. On what does ignorance rely? It arises in dependence upon suchness. To contemplate the ignorant mind is to contemplate the mind of suchness; to contemplate the mind-nature is to contemplate the ignorant mind. Why? Because suchness is the substance of thought, and thought is the function of suchness. To contemplate and thereby attain concentration is the samadhi of suchness, the king of all samadhis, and this is why it is called the supreme concentration.

What mind is to be contemplated? It is said: contemplate the ignorant mind. Why not contemplate the true mind? Because since the beginningless past the true mind has been perfumed and obscured by ignorance and cannot manifest. Where does this ignorance dwell? It dwells upon the true mind, like glue sticking to lacquer, never able to gain release; therefore it is called the ignorance that abides in the ground. This ignorance is the root of birth-and-death; while a single part of it remains unexhausted, birth-and-death forever continues, and so it is called fundamental ignorance. One who studies the Dharma and seeks the truth must begin with this ignorance that abides in the ground. Why? If when felling a tree one does not cut its root, or when treating an illness one does not strike the right point, then it avails nothing at all. Therefore those of the Two Vehicles and the bodhisattvas of the provisional teaching may sever the four abiding ignorances, yet they do not know the ignorance that abides in the ground; they can escape birth-and-death by divisions but in the end still undergo birth-and-death by transformation. One who follows the One Vehicle begins with contemplating the mind in order to break the ignorance that abides in the ground, so that birth-and-death is cut off forever; this is what is meant by drawing blood from the throat, the marvelous formula for becoming a Buddha, the most genuine and the most real. Elder Li says:
"Fundamental ignorance is none other than the fundamental, unmoving wisdom."
Yongjia says:
"The real nature of ignorance is itself the Buddha-nature."
The Tiantai school says:
"The substance of ignorance is itself illumination, itself reality, itself the Dharma-nature."

The scriptures quote this in endless profusion, and all point to this very point. At first, contemplate the mind that arises and ceases, without grasping or clinging, without following it or cutting it off; or give yourself over wholly to stilling thought and forgetting deliberation; and the two methods are one. (The Essentials of the Mind-Dharma Transmission says:
"Still thought and forget deliberation, and the Buddha appears of itself before you."

To contemplate and reflect constantly is to perfume ignorance with prajna. The very moment ignorance is broken, the dharmakaya suddenly manifests. In one leap one enters directly the ground of the Tathagata; without passing through asankhya kalpas one attains the dharmakaya; and so it is called the perfect and sudden gate of the Dharma.

Choose a clean and quiet place and sit in the full lotus posture. (First press the left foot upon the right thigh, then press the right foot upon the left thigh, so that the soles of both feet face upward upon the two thighs. Place the hands likewise, right over left, resting upon the upturned crossed legs. This is the full lotus, called the auspicious sitting. Or one may use only the half lotus, resting the right foot upon the left thigh, which is also acceptable. There is moreover the demon-subduing sitting: first press the right foot upon the left thigh, then the left foot upon the right thigh, with the hands left over right; the Chan school has for the most part transmitted this posture, so let each person choose as he wishes. The aged may sit upright and simple instead.) Keep the body upright and straight, neither moving nor swaying. Form the concentration mudra with the hands. (Turn both palms upward, the right hand placed over the left, the tips of the two thumbs touching, and rest them below the navel upon the crossed legs. This is called the dharma-realm concentration mudra, and it can dispel all wild and deluded thoughts.) Close the eyes to cut off the light, close the mouth and join the teeth, keep the tongue against the upper palate, and let the nose face the navel. Keep the spine straight as a rod and the two shoulders level, without leaning or tilting, and so sit.

For those busy with affairs, one must sit once a day, at least half an hour each time. If one can sit two or three times, each for an hour or two, that is even better. The more often and the longer, the better. When sitting, loosen the clothes and slacken the belt, calm and at ease, and do not sit in a draft, nor after a full meal. When the sitting is completed, gently move the body, slowly open the eyes and mouth, rub the two hands together until warm, and massage the face, eyes, waist, abdomen, legs, and feet; rest a while, and then rise.
Question: Because of the limitations of my body I am unable to sit in the lotus posture. What shall I do?

Answer: You may use the loose cross-legged position, with the two legs crossed, or sit upright upon a chair or stool; whatever the posture, keep the back straight, though without thrusting the chest out too far, and adopt the one that is stable and can be sustained for long.
Question: When contemplating the mind, must I always form the mudra?
Answer: One may contemplate the mind without forming the mudra.
Question: When the contemplation of mind is finished, to where should I dedicate the merit?

Answer: To contemplate the mind is itself the dedication of merit to the true reality of suchness, for the other Buddhas and one's own Buddha are one body; what further doubt could there be? Since you have newly entered the Dharma gate, dedicating the merit to the other Buddhas is also acceptable.

blocks.text: 5. Contemplating the Mind Off the Cushion

inline.s: In contemplating the mind, the crucial point is that it be continuous and unbroken, never forgotten. The ancients said:
"If a single thought is not present
(the thought of contemplation is not present)
, one is the same as a dead man."

The essential instruction of contemplating the mind is this: one can contemplate the mind anywhere at any time, and one is always contemplating the mind, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, never apart from the present thought, ever the master of oneself. When the practice reaches this point, its wonder is so deep and vast as to be without limit, like water drunk by a man, whose warmth and coolness he alone knows.
Question: How does one apply effort while in motion?

Answer: Just as when still. While contemplation of the mind is not yet mature, there is a distinction between motion and stillness. Once it is mature, motion and stillness are no different. The Chan school says:
"Amid ten thousand people, as though there were not a single person; amid the turmoil of ten thousand affairs, as though there were not a single affair."

From this one may know that motion and stillness are one. Beginners have not yet attained concentration, and so the patriarchs teach people to tend and carry, meaning that in dealing with affairs and meeting people one should always tend and carry along this method of contemplating the mind. You need not be concerned; with long practice it becomes clear of itself. I quote a passage from the Lankavatara Sutra, to have it ready for your use. The sutra says:
"Contemplate all dharmas as without self-nature: like clouds in the sky, like a whirling wheel of fire, like a city of gandharvas, like an illusion, like a mirage
(like a dream, like a heat-haze)

, like the moon in water, like what is seen in a dream, never apart from one's own mind. Because of beginningless false views, one takes them to be external. Having contemplated thus, cut off the conditions of discrimination, and be free as well of the names and meanings that the deluded mind grasps. Know that the body, and things, and the place where one dwells, are all the realm of the store consciousness. There is no one who takes, and nothing taken, no arising, abiding, or ceasing. Reflecting thus, abide in it forever without letting go."

Savor this passage of scripture in the heart, and deep faith will arise. That you have not been able to do so has two causes: first, you are not yet familiar with the doctrine; second, the power of concentration is not yet accomplished. In short, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you must never be apart from contemplation of the mind.
[Contemplating all dharmas as without self-nature]
Contemplate all dharmas: they are all phantasms.
The word self-nature has two meanings in Buddhist learning: first, the numinous power of wondrous illumination and myriad virtues
, and this is the self-nature of every living being and of every Buddha. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
"When self-nature is deluded, this is the living being; when self-nature is awakened, this is the Buddha."
(See
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathagatagarbha
; the second meaning is that of a real substance. The saying '
all

dharmas are without self-nature' means that all dharmas have no real substance and are all phantasms, like things in a dream. Being without self-nature is also called being without nature. The Treatise on Consciousness-Only says:
"All dharmas are without self-nature."
The Lotus Sutra says:
"Know that all dharmas are ever without nature."
The Surangama Sutra says:
"All phantasms become without nature."

[The whirling wheel of fire] In the darkness a man whirls a burning brand, and it is mistaken for a wheel of fire; this is used to illustrate a false appearance. [The city of gandharvas] The musicians are called gandharvas, and they can conjure towers and pavilions for people to behold; therefore these conjured towers are called a city of gandharvas. Phantasmal scenes such as a mirage over the sea are also called a city of gandharvas. [The heat-haze] The vapor produced beneath a blazing sun looks from afar like water; a thirsty deer longs to drink and runs after it, yet in the end can never reach it; this is used to illustrate an illusion. (See
Selected Notes on the Lankavatara Sutra

Question: I have already attained one mind undisturbed in reciting the Buddha-name, and I now study the White Cloud Essentials of Mind in order to realize the mind and see the nature. But contemplation of the mind cannot be sustained, and it is harder still to contemplate the mind whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. What shall I do?

Answer: You may proceed in two steps. First accomplish this: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, recite the Buddha-name without interruption and without distraction. Then raise a phrase of the Buddha-name and contemplate the mind for a while, raise the Buddha-name and contemplate for a while, and so on; in this way gradually pass over to complete contemplation of the mind, so that whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down you are never apart from contemplation of the mind.
